Chapter 6: Reflecting and Iterating — Building a Personal Feedback Loop.
Alright, so you’ve got your foundational habits down—you’re choosing a daily Highlight, managing your attention, cutting down distractions, and protecting your energy. But how do you actually know these habits are working for you?
That’s where reflection and iteration step in. Think of it like tuning a guitar. Even the best musicians need to stop and adjust their strings now and then, just to make sure everything’s sounding right. In your daily life, this means checking in with yourself to see how your routines are really serving you.
Here’s an easy way to start: set aside just a few minutes at the end of your day—or week—to pause and reflect. Ask yourself things like, "Did I actually accomplish my Highlight today? If not, what got in my way?" Or, "When did I feel most focused and full of energy? When did I feel scattered or totally drained?" Pay attention to which distractions were toughest to resist, and what strategies actually helped you stay on track.
You don’t have to write a novel; even jotting down a quick note, or just thinking through these questions, can reveal some surprising patterns over time. Maybe you’ll notice you’re always sharper in the morning, or that certain digital temptations just keep popping up.
Now, this kind of reflection naturally leads right into iteration—that’s just a fancy word for making small, targeted changes to your approach. You might try switching up your Highlight, choosing something a bit smaller and more specific if you keep feeling overwhelmed, or maybe going bigger if things are starting to feel a little too easy.
You can also play around with your Focus Blocks—maybe shift your deep work to a different part of the day, or test out shorter or longer sessions to see what really fits your rhythm.
And don’t forget your environment. Try rearranging your workspace, experiment with new background sounds, or set clearer boundaries with the people around you. Even energy habits can get a fresh spin—maybe add a quick walk after lunch, or try out a new bedtime routine.
The most important thing here? Treat every change like an experiment—not a judgment. There’s no such thing as a perfect system. What matters is that you’re learning what actually helps you show up feeling more present and purposeful. Over time, this feedback loop becomes a quiet source of wisdom, gently guiding you as your life and needs evolve.
